passages.title: Rotating shifts, sleep architecture and vigilance
paragraphs: Sleep is not a uniform state. Across a night a sleeper cycles through light non-rapid-eye-movement stages, a deeper slow-wave stage, and rapid-eye-movement sleep, and the proportions of each shift with the time of day at which sleep is attempted. Investigators recruited 72 hospital staff from a single teaching hospital and studied them after they had worked a particular rota for two consecutive weeks. Twenty-four worked days only. Twenty-four worked a slow rotation, in which the shift changed once every two weeks. Twenty-four worked a rapid rotation, in which the shift changed every second day. Staff were not assigned to a rota by the investigators; each had been placed on a rota by the hospital's scheduling office months earlier.

At the end of the two weeks each participant slept one night in a laboratory, beginning at the hour at which they would ordinarily have gone to bed. Electrodes recorded the electroencephalogram, eye movements and muscle tone, and a technician blind to rota scored each 30-second epoch as stage 1, 2 or 3 of non-rapid-eye-movement sleep, as rapid-eye-movement sleep, or as wake. On waking, participants completed a 10-minute vigilance task in which they pressed a key whenever a small dot appeared at an unpredictable interval; a response slower than 500 ms was counted as a lapse. Table 1 gives the mean minutes in each stage, the mean total sleep time, and the mean number of lapses.

The rapid-rotation group slept 80 minutes less in total than the day-only group, and recorded more than three times as many lapses. The investigators noted that the shortfall was not spread evenly across the stages, and that the stage most reduced is the one from which sleepers are hardest to wake. They argued that a rota which moves a worker's sleep period before the circadian system has adjusted to the previous move imposes a cost that no single night of recovery sleep repays.

figure.caption: Table 1  Mean minutes per stage, total sleep time and vigilance lapses, by rota.

passages.title: Two routes into early vocabulary
paragraphs: Children differ widely in how many words they produce at two and a half years, and the input they hear differs widely too. Two features of that input are often confused. The first is sheer quantity: how many words an adult speaks near the child in an hour. The second is contingency: how often an adult answers what the child has just done or said, promptly and on the same topic. Investigators followed 96 children recruited from nurseries in one city. At 18 months each family wore a recorder for two full days at home. Trained coders transcribed six randomly chosen hours per family and counted adult words per hour, and separately the proportion of the child's own vocalisations that drew an adult reply within two seconds on the same topic.

Families also reported hours of television audible in the room per day, and parents completed a checklist of words the child produced. At 30 months the same checklist was completed again, and the number of words produced was the study's outcome. Coders were blind to the families' 18-month vocabulary scores. Table 1 gives the correlation of each 18-month measure with vocabulary at 30 months, together with the correlation of contingent replies with 30-month vocabulary after adult words per hour had been partialled out.

Quantity and contingency were themselves correlated with each other at r = 0.39, so a family that spoke more also tended to reply more. The investigators argued that the two are nevertheless separable, and that the second carries most of the association with later vocabulary. They were careful to say that no family had been assigned to speak in one way rather than another, and that nothing in the design rules out a third variable that raises both contingent replying and the child's own rate of word learning.

passages.title: Tokens, schedules and persistence in a classroom
paragraphs: A reading programme in one school issued plastic tokens that children could exchange for time in the library. Investigators used the programme to compare three schedules of reinforcement. Sixty children aged 9 and 10 were assigned at random to one of three groups of 20. In the fixed-ratio group a token arrived after every tenth page read. In the variable-ratio group a token arrived after an average of ten pages, but the number required varied unpredictably from two to eighteen. In the fixed-interval group a token arrived for the first page completed after each two minutes of reading had elapsed. All three groups read in daily 20-minute sessions for three weeks, and by the final session of the token phase the three groups were reading an equal mean of 45 pages per session.

Tokens were then withdrawn without announcement. The sessions continued unchanged in every other respect for four further days. Figure 1 shows the mean pages read per session for each group in the last token session and in each of the four withdrawal sessions. Teachers recorded the pages read and knew which schedule each child had been on.

Reading fell in all three groups once the tokens stopped, but not at the same rate. By the fourth withdrawal session the variable-ratio group was still reading 29 pages per session, about 64 percent of its token-phase level, while the fixed-ratio group had fallen to 9. The investigators argued that what a schedule teaches is not only how often to respond but also what the absence of a reinforcer means. Under a fixed schedule a missing token is an informative event, because the child has learned exactly when one is due. Under a variable schedule no particular page is the one that pays, so a run of unrewarded pages is nothing a child has not met before.

figure.caption: Figure 1  Mean pages read per session in the last token session (T) and the four withdrawal sessions. Solid line, variable ratio; dashed line, fixed ratio; dotted line, fixed interval.

passages.title: Eight weeks of two treatments for low mood
paragraphs: Two hundred and forty adults presenting to primary care with moderate depressive symptoms consented to a trial. A score of 24 or more on a 60-point symptom inventory was required for entry. Patients were allocated by a computer-generated sequence, concealed from the recruiting clinician, to one of three arms of 80. The first arm received a structured behavioural activation programme of eight weekly sessions, in which patients scheduled and recorded small activities they had stopped doing. The second received a standard antidepressant at a fixed dose. The third was placed on a waiting list and offered the programme after the trial ended.

Symptoms were scored at entry and at week eight by assessors who were not told which arm a patient had been allocated to. A patient was counted as a responder if their score fell by at least half. Table 1 gives the number allocated and the number still attending at week eight, the mean symptom score at each time point, and the proportion of responders in each arm. Patients who stopped attending were telephoned and, where they agreed, scored at week eight at home.

The three arms began at effectively the same mean score. By week eight both active arms had separated from the waiting list, and the behavioural programme had the highest proportion of responders. The waiting-list arm also improved, from a mean of 32 to a mean of 28, which the investigators took as a reason that no uncontrolled before-and-after comparison could have settled the question. Attendance differed across the arms, with the antidepressant arm losing the most patients, and the investigators reported that most of those who left that arm cited side effects in the first fortnight.

passages.title: Dose, symptom cluster and side effect in first-episode psychosis
paragraphs: Antipsychotic drugs in common use block dopamine D2 receptors, and the clinical question is how much blockade is worth its cost. A clinic followed 120 patients presenting with a first episode of psychosis. Each was rated on two subscales of a standard interview, one covering positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions and one covering negative symptoms such as blunted affect, poverty of speech and loss of volition. Each subscale runs from 0 to 30, with higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. Patients were allocated at random to a low, standard or high fixed dose of the same D2 antagonist and rated again after six weeks by an interviewer who did not know the dose.

A third scale recorded movement side effects of the kind attributed to blockade of dopamine pathways outside the limbic system, on a 0 to 30 scale. Table 1 gives the mean score on each measure at entry and at six weeks. The three groups were well matched at entry, with identical mean subscale scores.

Positive symptoms fell at every dose, and fell further as the dose rose. Negative symptoms barely moved at any dose, and did not move at all at the high dose. Movement side effects rose steeply with dose, from a mean of 2 at the low dose to a mean of 11 at the high dose. The clinicians concluded that the drug acts on one symptom cluster rather than on the disorder as a whole, and that the step from the standard to the high dose bought a single further point of positive-symptom improvement at a considerable cost. They added that the negative cluster, which predicts long-term functioning better than the positive cluster does, was left essentially untouched.

passages.title: Goal specificity, a watched model and persistence at a puzzle
paragraphs: A laboratory task was used to separate two things that often travel together: what a person is asked to achieve, and what they believe they can achieve. One hundred and fifty undergraduates were told they would work through a set of letter puzzles of graded difficulty for 25 minutes. Before any instruction was given, each rated on a 1 to 10 scale how confident they were that they could solve puzzles of this kind. That rating is the baseline confidence column of Table 1.

Participants were then assigned at random to one of four conditions. The do-your-best group was asked simply to do as well as they could. The easy-goal group was asked to solve eight puzzles. The difficult-goal group was asked to solve sixteen. The fourth group received the same difficult goal, but first watched a two-minute recording in which a student of their own age worked through two puzzles aloud, got one wrong, said what she would try next, and solved it. The model left the recording before the participant began, and no participant worked in the presence of another person.

The investigators recorded the number of puzzles solved, and the number of minutes a participant kept working after reaching a puzzle they could not solve, which was the study's measure of persistence. At the end, participants rated their confidence again on the same scale. Table 1 gives the means. Baseline confidence was flat across the four conditions and bore no relation to the number of puzzles a group went on to solve. Confidence measured after the task told a different story: it rose by more than a point in both difficult-goal conditions and by two tenths of a point in the other two. The investigators argued that a specific and demanding target changes effort, and that watching someone else struggle and recover changes what a person expects effort to accomplish.

passages.title: How a test is described and how it is taken
paragraphs: Performance on a test is not fixed by what a person knows. Investigators prepared a 20-item quantitative test of a difficulty the participating students had met in coursework, and administered it under a 20-minute limit. One hundred and eighty students were assigned at random to one of four cells formed by crossing two factors. The first factor was how the test was introduced. Half were told it was a diagnostic measure of mathematical ability that reliably distinguishes strong from weak students. Half were told it was a set of problem-solving puzzles being piloted for a later study, and that individual scores would not be examined.

The second factor was when a short demographic form, asking for age, sex and ethnic background, was placed. Half completed it immediately before the test and half immediately after. Every cell contained 45 students, every cell had the same 20 minutes, and the demographic form took under a minute in all cells and was timed separately so that it took no time from the test. Prior course grades were recorded from the registry and did not differ across the four cells. Table 1 gives the mean number of items answered correctly.

The two factors did not act independently. Where the test was called a diagnostic measure of ability, students who had just given their demographic details scored 9.8 against 12.6 for those who gave them afterwards. Where the same test was called a set of puzzles, the order of the form made almost no difference, 12.4 against 12.8. In a free-response item afterwards, several students in the low-scoring cell wrote that the test was not the sort of thing they were good at, and that they had been thinking during the test about how their answers would be read.

passages.title: Group size and intervention in a staged emergency
paragraphs: One hundred and sixty adults arrived individually for what they understood to be a study of consumer preferences. Each was shown to a waiting room and given a questionnaire. After four minutes a recording was played from an adjoining room: a crash of equipment, then a voice calling for help and saying that something had fallen on them. The recording ran for two minutes and then stopped. An observer behind a one-way screen timed how long it took the participant to leave the room or call out, and whether they did so at all within the two minutes.

Participants were assigned at random to one of four conditions of 40. In the first they waited alone. In the second, two other people were in the room; in the third, five were. Those others were confederates instructed to glance up at the sound, then return to their questionnaires and remain seated. The fourth condition also had five others, but one of them was instructed to put down the questionnaire at the first sound, look towards the wall and say nothing further. Table 1 gives the proportion who intervened and the mean time taken by those who did.

Intervention fell as the number of people in the room rose, and the time taken rose with it. The fourth condition shows that the number present was not the whole story. A single person who visibly treated the sound as worth attending to raised intervention from 31 percent to 62 percent without changing how many people were in the room. In a debriefing interview, participants in the five-other condition most often said that they had assumed someone else had already gone to help or had already telephoned for help, and several said that because nobody else had moved they had taken the sound to be part of the study.

passages.title: Ties, support and reported health in two neighbourhoods
paragraphs: A survey of 1,400 adults was drawn from two adjacent neighbourhoods of one city, one with a median household income roughly twice that of the other. Interviewers asked each respondent how many people they could call on to discuss something that mattered to them, how often they met those people, and whether they belonged to any club, congregation or association that met at least monthly. Respondents also rated their own health on a five-point scale, and completed a short screening questionnaire for depressive symptoms. Every measure was taken in the same interview.

Table 1 groups respondents by the number of close ties reported and gives, for each band, the proportion rating their health as good or excellent and the proportion screening positive on the depression questionnaire. The association ran in the same direction in both neighbourhoods. Respondents who belonged to an association meeting at least monthly rated their health as good or excellent 62 percent of the time, against 48 percent of those who did not, and membership was markedly less common in the lower-income neighbourhood, where fewer such associations met within walking distance.

The investigators were explicit about what the design could and could not support. Ties and health had been measured at the same moment from the same respondent, so an association between them is open to being read in either direction, and to being produced by something that bears on both. They noted that the resources which flow through a network, from a lift to a clinic to a word about a job, are unevenly distributed because the institutions through which ties are formed are unevenly distributed, and that a person's stock of such resources is therefore not simply a matter of how sociable they are.

passages.title: Segregation and primary-care supply in one county
paragraphs: Where people live is not independent of the services they can reach. Analysts assembled administrative records for the 148 census tracts of a single county. For each tract they recorded the share of residents belonging to the county's largest minority group, the number of primary-care physicians with a practice address in the tract per 10,000 residents, the share of adults reporting a usual source of medical care, and the number of hospital admissions per 1,000 residents for conditions that timely outpatient care is generally held to prevent. Tracts were then sorted into three bands by the first of these measures.

Table 1 gives the mean of each remaining measure within each band. Physician supply in the most segregated band was about a third of the supply in the least segregated band, and admissions for the conditions in question were more than twice as high. The analysts repeated the comparison after adjusting each tract's admission figure for the share of its residents without health insurance, and reported that the gradient across the bands was reduced but still present.

The analysts cautioned that the unit of analysis is the tract rather than the person, so a difference between bands need not hold of any particular resident, and that the share of one group's residents in a tract is a crude summary of a pattern that is better captured by measures of how evenly two populations are distributed across all the tracts of a city. They nevertheless argued that a practice chooses its address, that addresses follow the concentration of insured and higher-income patients, and that the resulting map is a structural feature of the county rather than an aggregate of individual choices about seeking care.
